lessons.title: Containers, images & runtimes
body: A container packages an application with its user-space dependencies. Linux containers share the host kernel, while a virtual machine runs its own guest operating system. This makes containers efficient, but does not make a container equivalent to a complete VM or a perfect security boundary.

An image is an immutable, layered template. A running container adds writable state. A registry stores images; a runtime starts and manages containers. OCI defines image and runtime specifications. Kubernetes communicates with compatible runtimes such as containerd and CRI-O through the Container Runtime Interface (CRI).

For a Nutanix infrastructure team, think of worker nodes as machines that could run on AHV. Kubernetes schedules Pods onto those nodes; it does not replace the hypervisor. Image tags can move, while a digest identifies specific image content.
remember: CRI connects Kubernetes to runtimes; OCI defines standards
Namespaces isolate views; cgroups control resource usage
lessons.trap: Docker-built images can run on Kubernetes without Docker Engine being the node runtime.
lessons.exercise: Explain image, registry and runtime to a colleague without using the word Docker.

lessons.title: The control plane & worker nodes
body: A Kubernetes cluster has a control plane and worker nodes. The API server exposes the Kubernetes API. Clients and components use that API to read or change cluster objects. etcd is the backing store for cluster state, not a database for your business application.

The scheduler selects a suitable node for an unscheduled Pod. Controllers repeatedly compare desired state with observed state and act to reduce differences. For example, if a Deployment needs three replicas and one disappears, its controllers create a replacement.

On each worker, the kubelet ensures that assigned Pods run through the container runtime. The networking implementation provides Service traffic routing, commonly using kube-proxy or an alternative implementation. The scheduler chooses a node; the kubelet manages execution there.
lessons.trap: The scheduler does not start containers itself.
lessons.exercise: Draw the path: kubectl → API server → scheduling → kubelet → runtime. Say where desired state is stored.

lessons.title: Objects, YAML & reconciliation
body: An API object describes something in the cluster. Common manifest fields include apiVersion, kind, metadata and spec. The spec expresses desired state. Status describes what the system has observed and is normally maintained by Kubernetes.

Declarative management means submitting the desired outcome and allowing controllers to reconcile it. Imperative commands describe individual actions. kubectl apply can manage a declarative manifest; repeatedly applying a consistent desired state should converge on that state.

Labels are key-value identifiers used to select related objects. Annotations hold non-identifying metadata. A Service selector can match labels on Pods. A label mismatch is a common reason for a Service to have no usable endpoints.
remember: Labels support selection; annotations hold metadata
Reconciliation is ongoing, not a one-time script
lessons.trap: YAML indentation matters, but KCNA preparation should focus on what the object means.
lessons.exercise: Read a Deployment manifest and point out its name, desired replicas, image and Pod labels.

lessons.title: Pods & container lifecycle
body: A Pod is the smallest deployable Kubernetes unit. One or more closely coupled containers share its network namespace and can share volumes. Containers in the same Pod can communicate using localhost; separate Pods have separate network identities.

Pods are disposable. A replacement Pod is a new object and may have a new IP address. A controller manages replacement, and a Service provides a stable access point. A bare Pod is not automatically recreated as a new Pod after its node is lost.

Init containers normally complete in order before application containers start. A sidecar supports the main application, for example by forwarding logs or proxying traffic. Do not put unrelated services together just because they can share a Pod.
remember: Pod containers share an IP and port space
Pod IPs are not durable service addresses
Use controllers for replacement and scaling
lessons.trap: A container restart inside a Pod is different from replacing the whole Pod.
lessons.exercise: Explain why two independent web applications usually belong in separate Pods.

lessons.title: Choose the right workload controller
body: A Deployment manages replicated applications and supports controlled rollouts, usually through ReplicaSets. It is a common choice for stateless services. A ReplicaSet maintains a requested number of matching Pods.

A StatefulSet gives Pods stable identities and supports stable storage association and ordered behavior. Use it when identity and persistent state matter. It does not automatically make a database highly available or back up its data.

A DaemonSet places a Pod on each eligible node, useful for node agents. A Job runs work to completion. A CronJob creates Jobs on a schedule. Choose based on the required behavior: replicas, identity, per-node presence, completion or scheduling.
remember: Deployment: replicated app; StatefulSet: stable identity
Job: finish work; CronJob: scheduled work
lessons.trap: A CronJob schedules Jobs, not worker nodes.
lessons.exercise: Map these needs: web frontend, log agent, nightly report, database replicas and one-off migration.

lessons.title: Namespaces, contexts & kubectl
body: Namespaces group namespaced API resources. Teams can use them to organize workloads, apply quotas and scope access. Namespaces do not by themselves provide complete network isolation. Nodes and PersistentVolumes are examples of cluster-scoped resources.

A kubeconfig stores cluster connection details, users and contexts. A context selects a cluster, identity and optional default namespace. Check it before issuing commands, particularly if your team manages multiple environments.

Know the intent of kubectl get, describe, logs, exec, apply and delete. get lists resources, describe reveals details and events, logs reads container output, and exec runs a command inside a container. Read-only inspection should come before making changes.
remember: Namespaces organize resources, not virtual machines
lessons.trap: Changing the namespace does not switch clusters.
lessons.exercise: In a disposable learning cluster, run kubectl config current-context and kubectl get pods -A. Explain each output.

lessons.title: Scheduling & resource management
body: The scheduler filters and scores nodes for unscheduled Pods. It considers resource requests and placement rules. CPU and memory requests guide placement; limits constrain usage. A node can appear idle but still lack enough unallocated requested resources for a Pod.

nodeSelector matches node labels. Node affinity provides more expressive placement rules. Taints repel Pods unless they have suitable tolerations. A toleration allows a Pod to be considered for a node; it does not guarantee that the Pod will land there.

CPU limits can cause throttling. Exceeding a memory limit can lead to termination for out-of-memory usage. ResourceQuota constrains aggregate consumption in a namespace, while LimitRange can provide per-object defaults and bounds.
remember: Requests influence scheduling; limits constrain usage
Toleration permits placement; affinity influences selection
Pending often points to placement or storage constraints
lessons.trap: A toleration is not an instruction to schedule on one specific node.
lessons.exercise: A Pod requests 8 GiB but each node has only 4 GiB available for requests. Explain why adding a CPU limit will not fix scheduling.

lessons.title: Configuration, Secrets & scaling
body: A ConfigMap separates non-confidential configuration from an image. A Secret stores sensitive values for use by workloads. Base64 encoding is not encryption. Secret safety also depends on access controls, encryption configuration and careful handling.

Configuration can be exposed as environment variables or mounted files. Updating a ConfigMap does not automatically update environment variables inside an already running process. Some mounted file updates propagate, but the application must still reload them as needed.

The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler changes replica counts using observed metrics. A node autoscaler changes available node capacity. These address different problems: more application instances versus more places to run them. Reliable metrics and meaningful resource requests are important for utilization-based scaling.
remember: ConfigMap: non-sensitive configuration; Secret: sensitive data
lessons.trap: Scaling Pods is not the same as increasing each Pod’s CPU or memory.
lessons.exercise: Choose where to store a log level and a database password. Explain what happens to existing environment variables after a change.

lessons.title: Services, DNS & traffic paths
body: A Service gives a stable network abstraction for reaching a changing set of Pods. ClusterIP is the usual internal-only Service type. NodePort exposes a port on nodes, while LoadBalancer integrates with an implementation that provides an external load balancer.

Cluster DNS lets workloads discover Services by name. A Service usually selects Pods using labels; EndpointSlices track the relevant endpoints. If connectivity fails, check selectors, Pod readiness, ports and DNS before assuming the network is broken.

An Ingress describes HTTP/HTTPS routing rules and needs an Ingress controller to implement them. A Service is not itself a layer-7 URL router. NetworkPolicy defines permitted traffic where supported by the networking plugin; creating a namespace alone does not enforce it.
remember: Service: stable access to changing Pods
DNS names are preferable to hard-coded Pod IPs
lessons.trap: Declaring a LoadBalancer Service does not guarantee an external IP on every cluster.
lessons.exercise: Trace browser → load balancer/Ingress controller → Service → ready Pod.

lessons.title: CNI, CSI, CRI & service meshes
body: Kubernetes relies on extension interfaces. CRI connects kubelet to container runtimes. CNI is used by networking plugins for container networking. CSI allows storage providers to integrate volume operations. Match the acronym to the concern before learning individual products.

A service mesh adds capabilities to service-to-service communication such as traffic policies, telemetry and workload identity. Some designs use sidecars; others use different data-plane architectures. Kubernetes does not require a mesh for basic networking.

Keep responsibility boundaries clear. A container runtime launches containers. A network plugin connects Pods. A storage driver handles volume operations. A mesh controls application traffic behavior above the basic network.
remember: CRI = runtime; CNI = networking; CSI = storage
lessons.trap: CSI does not schedule Pods and CNI does not pull images.
lessons.exercise: For an AHV-hosted cluster with a volume mount problem, identify the Kubernetes interface you would investigate first.

lessons.title: Authentication, RBAC & least privilege
body: Authentication answers who is making the request. Authorization decides what that identity may do. Admission control then validates or mutates applicable requests before persistence. A successful login does not imply permission to list every resource.

RBAC rules specify API groups, resources and verbs. Roles are namespaced. ClusterRoles can express cluster-scoped rules or reusable namespaced rules. A RoleBinding grants permissions within its namespace, including when it refers to a ClusterRole; a ClusterRoleBinding grants them across the cluster.

ServiceAccounts provide workload identities. Prefer narrow permissions and dedicated identities. Do not give a backup process cluster-admin merely because it needs to read selected resources. In a Nutanix context, this is similar in intent to separating operational roles, but Kubernetes RBAC is a separate authorization system.
lessons.trap: Referencing a ClusterRole from a RoleBinding does not automatically grant cluster-wide access.
lessons.exercise: Define the smallest permissions needed by a tool that only lists Pods in a single namespace.

lessons.title: Workload & supply-chain security
body: Use trusted images, scan for known vulnerabilities and keep dependencies current. Prefer immutable references for reproducibility. Image signing and provenance help establish where software came from; they do not prove that it has no vulnerabilities.

Run workloads with the privileges they need. Common controls include non-root execution, dropping Linux capabilities, a read-only root filesystem and preventing privilege escalation. Pod Security admission can enforce Pod Security Standards at namespace level.

NetworkPolicy can restrict ingress and egress for selected Pods when enforced by the networking implementation. TLS protects traffic in transit. Neither a namespace nor a base64-encoded Secret substitutes for these controls.
remember: Least privilege applies to API access and container execution
lessons.trap: An image with no known CVEs today is not guaranteed safe forever.
lessons.exercise: Review a sample manifest for privileged mode, root user, unnecessary mounts and broad permissions.

lessons.title: Volumes, PVs, PVCs & StorageClasses
body: Container writable filesystems are ephemeral. Volumes provide storage to containers in a Pod. emptyDir lasts with the Pod and can survive an individual container restart, but is lost when the Pod is removed.

A PersistentVolume (PV) represents storage in the cluster. A PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC) requests storage for a workload. A StorageClass describes a class of storage and commonly enables dynamic provisioning through a driver. The Pod consumes the PVC; the claim binds to a suitable volume.

For an infrastructure team, separate the backing storage platform from its Kubernetes objects. CSI bridges to storage capabilities; a PVC is the application’s request. ReadWriteOnce generally permits read-write mounting by a single node, not necessarily a single Pod. Reclaim policy affects what happens to storage after a claim is released.
remember: PVC requests; PV provides; StorageClass describes provisioning
emptyDir is tied to Pod lifetime
lessons.trap: ReadWriteOnce does not mean one Pod in all circumstances.
lessons.exercise: Explain why a database needs persistent storage even if Kubernetes can recreate its Pod.

lessons.title: Troubleshoot by symptoms
body: Work from evidence. For Pending, inspect events for resource constraints, placement rules or unbound storage. For ImagePullBackOff, inspect image names, tags, registry access and pull credentials. For CrashLoopBackOff, inspect the application’s logs, exit reason, configuration and probes.

Use kubectl describe pod for events and container state. kubectl logs --previous can reveal output from the previous terminated container instance. If a Service has no traffic, inspect its selectors, EndpointSlices, target port and readiness state.

Separate infrastructure symptoms from application symptoms. An HTTP 500 can indicate an application problem even when the network path works. A DNS lookup failure has different evidence from a process that cannot open its configuration file. Avoid deleting resources before collecting useful evidence.
remember: Collect events and logs before changing state
lessons.trap: BackOff describes retry behavior; it is not the underlying root cause.
lessons.exercise: Choose the first two checks for a Pending Pod and for a repeatedly crashing Pod.

lessons.title: CI/CD & immutable delivery
body: Continuous integration builds and tests frequent code changes. Continuous delivery keeps a change ready for release, often with a manual production approval. Continuous deployment automatically releases changes that pass the required checks.

A typical pipeline tests code, builds an image, scans it, publishes it and updates deployment configuration. Build once and promote the same immutable artifact through environments. Rebuilding separately for production can introduce differences from what was tested.

Kubernetes handles workload orchestration; it is not a complete source-code build system. Tooling such as CI runners, registries and delivery controllers supplies the other stages. Health checks and observability help determine whether a release is actually working.
remember: CI builds/tests; CD delivers or deploys
A successful build does not prove a healthy release
lessons.trap: Continuous delivery and continuous deployment differ at the production release decision.
lessons.exercise: Sketch your team’s path from a code commit to a healthy running application.

lessons.title: GitOps, drift & reconciliation
body: GitOps stores desired system state declaratively in version control. An agent pulls that state and reconciles the running environment toward it. Reviewable commits provide change history and a place to apply team approval practices.

Argo CD and Flux are examples of GitOps tooling. A running cluster can drift when someone makes an out-of-band change. A configured controller can detect the difference and, depending on policy, reconcile it. GitOps is more than putting a script in a Git repository.

Reverting a configuration commit can restore earlier desired state, but that does not automatically reverse database migrations or data changes. Secrets require a deliberate secure workflow; a private repository alone is not sufficient protection for plaintext credentials.
remember: GitOps detects differences between desired and live state
lessons.trap: GitOps does not mean every git push must deploy immediately without review.
lessons.exercise: A manual replica change keeps reverting. Explain what a GitOps controller might be doing.

lessons.title: Rollouts, Helm & release strategies
body: A rolling update gradually replaces old replicas with new ones. maxSurge permits temporary extra Pods, while maxUnavailable limits unavailable replicas. Readiness determines whether a Pod should receive Service traffic.

Blue-green delivery keeps old and new environments and switches traffic. Canary delivery exposes a limited audience or traffic fraction to a new version before wider rollout. These strategies require appropriate traffic control and useful health signals; a Deployment alone does not provide every advanced traffic-splitting behavior.

Helm packages related Kubernetes manifests into charts with configurable values. A release is an installed chart instance. Kustomize applies overlays to base manifests. Both help manage configuration, but neither eliminates the need to understand the underlying Kubernetes resources.
remember: Rolling: gradual replacement; canary: limited exposure
lessons.trap: A rollout can complete while the application still has a functional bug.
lessons.exercise: Pick a strategy for testing a risky feature with 5% of traffic, and explain the signal you would monitor.

lessons.title: Probes & application debugging
body: A readiness probe determines whether a container is ready to serve traffic. Failing readiness normally removes the Pod from matching Service endpoints without restarting the container. A liveness probe detects when restarting a container may help. A startup probe protects slow startup by delaying liveness and readiness probing until startup succeeds.

Probe design matters. A liveness check that fails whenever an external dependency is unavailable can trigger unnecessary restart loops. Readiness can be used to stop new traffic while the application is temporarily unable to serve it.

For a failed release, inspect rollout status, events, image changes, configuration and logs. Compare the new version with the last healthy one. kubectl rollout undo can restore a Deployment revision, but persistent data and external dependencies may still need separate recovery.
lessons.trap: Readiness failure does not itself restart a container.
lessons.exercise: A Java service takes two minutes to start and is killed repeatedly after 30 seconds. Which probe design needs attention?

lessons.title: Metrics, logs, traces & OpenTelemetry
body: Metrics are numerical measurements over time, useful for rates, counts and distributions. Logs record events. Distributed traces connect spans across a request’s path through services. Use them together: an error-rate metric shows a trend, a trace identifies the slow service, and logs add local context.

Prometheus collects and queries time-series metrics, commonly by scraping endpoints. Grafana visualizes data from multiple sources. OpenTelemetry supplies vendor-neutral instrumentation and telemetry collection/export building blocks; it is not itself a complete storage and dashboard backend.

A service-level indicator (SLI) measures user-facing behavior. A service-level objective (SLO) sets a target for that indicator. An error budget expresses tolerated unreliability over a period. Alert on actionable symptoms rather than every harmless transient fluctuation.
remember: Metrics: how much; logs: events; traces: request path
lessons.trap: A trace is not simply a long log file, and OpenTelemetry is not a dashboard product.
lessons.exercise: For high checkout latency, choose a metric, a trace and a log entry that would each help.

lessons.title: Cloud native principles & trade-offs
body: Cloud native systems use patterns such as declarative automation, loosely coupled services and resilient infrastructure to make changes more safely and frequently. Running on a public cloud is not a requirement: cloud native workloads can run on premises, including on infrastructure managed by your team.

Microservices can enable independent deployment and scaling, but introduce network calls, distributed failure modes and operational overhead. A well-designed modular monolith may be the better choice for some teams. Containers alone do not make an architecture resilient.

Design for failure: use redundancy, timeouts, bounded retries and graceful degradation where appropriate. Horizontal scaling adds instances; vertical scaling increases resources per instance. Serverless abstracts more infrastructure operations but does not remove the servers underneath.
remember: Cloud native is an operating approach, not a hosting location
Resilience must be designed and observed
Microservices create trade-offs, not automatic benefits
lessons.trap: Moving an unchanged VM to public cloud is not by itself a cloud native transformation.
lessons.exercise: Describe one benefit and one operational cost of splitting a monolith into services.

lessons.title: CNCF projects & open-source collaboration
body: The Cloud Native Computing Foundation supports a vendor-neutral ecosystem of projects and communities. Learn what categories of tools do before memorizing logos: orchestration, runtimes, networking, storage, observability and delivery.

Project maturity levels include Sandbox, Incubating and Graduated. They reflect project and community maturity criteria; they are not a promise that a project is the best fit for every workload. Consult the live CNCF landscape when making actual product choices because status can change.

Open-source collaboration includes issue reports, documentation, reviews, testing and code. Follow each project’s contribution guide and code of conduct. Kubernetes SIGs focus on particular subject areas. A useful issue includes a reproducible problem, environment details and relevant sanitized evidence.
remember: Know tool purpose before project trivia
Documentation and testing are valid contributions
lessons.trap: CNCF membership does not mean every member product is a CNCF-hosted project.
lessons.exercise: Find a project contribution guide and describe a useful non-code contribution your team could make.

questions.question: Which component selects a node for a newly created Pod?
questions.explanation: The scheduler selects placement. The kubelet then manages execution on the selected node.

questions.question: Where is Kubernetes cluster state persistently stored?
questions.explanation: etcd stores Kubernetes API state; a registry stores images and logs capture application output.

questions.question: An application needs three interchangeable web replicas and rolling updates. Which resource fits?
questions.explanation: Deployments manage replicated applications and controlled rollouts through ReplicaSets.

questions.question: What is the smallest deployable unit managed by Kubernetes?
questions.explanation: Kubernetes schedules Pods, which can contain one or more closely coupled containers.

questions.question: Two containers in one Pod need to communicate. Which address is normally appropriate?
options: A different node IP for each container
questions.explanation: Containers in a Pod share its network namespace and can communicate using localhost.

questions.question: A node agent must run on every eligible worker. Which controller fits?
questions.explanation: DaemonSets maintain a Pod on each eligible node, including suitable new nodes.

questions.question: Which resource runs a task to completion?
questions.explanation: A Job tracks successful completion. A Service exposes workloads rather than executing a task.

questions.question: Which object creates Jobs according to a time schedule?
questions.explanation: A CronJob creates Jobs on a schedule; it does not perform node placement.

questions.question: What does an object's spec normally express?
questions.explanation: spec holds the requested configuration. status reports observed state.

questions.question: Which metadata is designed for selecting a group of related Pods?
questions.explanation: Labels are identifying key-value metadata that selectors can match.

questions.question: Which metadata is suitable for a build-system reference that should not select Pods?
questions.explanation: Annotations hold non-identifying metadata; labels are used for selection.

questions.question: What is a container image?
options: A layered template used to create containers
questions.explanation: An image supplies packaged files and metadata. A running container is an instance using it.

questions.question: Which statement best distinguishes typical Linux containers from VMs?
options: Every container includes a separate guest kernel
Containers never need an operating system
questions.explanation: Containers isolate processes while sharing a kernel; VMs typically run guest kernels.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of an image registry?
questions.explanation: A registry distributes images to clients and runtimes; it does not schedule workloads.

questions.question: Which resource gives a replicated workload stable Pod identities?
questions.explanation: StatefulSets provide stable identities and storage associations; they do not automatically replicate application data.

questions.question: A Pod requests more memory than any node has available for requests. What is the likely result?
options: The registry creates a larger node
questions.explanation: Resource requests guide placement. No feasible node means the scheduler cannot place it.

questions.question: What does a toleration do?
options: Allows a Pod to tolerate a matching taint
Guarantees placement on a particular node
questions.explanation: Toleration removes a taint-based exclusion; other scheduling constraints still apply.

questions.question: Which object holds non-confidential application settings?
questions.explanation: ConfigMaps separate ordinary configuration from images. Sensitive values belong in a secured Secret workflow.

questions.question: What does base64 encoding provide for a Secret value?
questions.explanation: Base64 is encoding, not encryption. Access and encryption controls must be configured separately.

questions.question: What does the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler primarily adjust?
questions.explanation: HPA changes replicas using metrics. Node autoscaling adjusts cluster capacity.

questions.question: Which command is most useful for Pod details and recent events?
questions.explanation: describe shows object details and events, often exposing scheduling or startup problems.

questions.question: What does a kubeconfig context select?
options: Cluster, identity and optional default namespace
questions.explanation: Contexts choose the connection and identity used by kubectl, plus an optional namespace.

questions.question: A Deployment requests four replicas and one Pod disappears. What behavior should you expect?
options: Its controllers work to create a replacement
The scheduler restores the old Pod's filesystem
questions.explanation: Controllers reconcile observed state toward desired replicas. The replacement is a new Pod.

questions.question: Which node component ensures assigned Pod containers run?
questions.explanation: The kubelet manages assigned Pods through the runtime; the scheduler only chooses placement.

questions.question: Which interface connects kubelet to a compatible container runtime?
questions.explanation: CRI is the Container Runtime Interface. CSI concerns storage and CNI networking.

questions.question: Which project defines interoperable container image and runtime specifications?
questions.explanation: The Open Container Initiative defines image and runtime specifications, distinct from Kubernetes runtime integration.

questions.question: Why prefer an image digest for reproducible releases?
options: It always makes the image smaller
questions.explanation: Tags can move; a digest identifies immutable content. It does not imply vulnerability-free software.

questions.question: A bare Pod is lost with its node. What is missing if you expect a replacement Pod?
questions.explanation: Controllers such as Deployments create replacements. A bare Pod lacks that replication behavior.

questions.question: Which statement about a replacement Pod is correct?
options: It always keeps the previous Pod IP
It is the same object with the same UID
It is a new object and may get a new IP
questions.explanation: Pod identity and ephemeral storage do not survive replacement; use Services and persistent volumes as needed.

questions.question: Which container usually finishes prerequisite setup before application containers start?
questions.explanation: Regular init containers run to completion before application containers start.

questions.question: Which use case best fits a sidecar?
options: A helper forwarding the main application's logs
questions.explanation: A sidecar supports the main application and shares the Pod lifecycle and context.

questions.question: A Pod manifest has kind, metadata and spec but no API version. Which field is missing?
questions.explanation: apiVersion identifies the API group/version for the object along with kind.

questions.question: Which approach is declarative?
options: Edit a container's filesystem by hand
Copy files to each worker interactively
Submit a manifest expressing three desired replicas
questions.explanation: Declarative configuration states the desired outcome for controllers to maintain.

questions.question: Which resource is cluster-scoped?
questions.explanation: Nodes belong to the cluster rather than a namespace. Pods, ConfigMaps and Secrets are namespaced.

questions.question: What does kubectl get pods -A request?
options: All container images from a registry
questions.explanation: -A selects all namespaces for a namespaced resource listing.

questions.question: Which action should precede commands in a multi-cluster environment?
questions.explanation: Checking context prevents actions against the wrong cluster or identity.

questions.question: A CPU limit is repeatedly reached. What can happen?
questions.explanation: CPU usage can be throttled by limits; memory-limit enforcement can instead lead to OOM termination.

questions.question: What can happen when a container exceeds its memory limit?
options: It may be terminated for out-of-memory usage
questions.explanation: Memory limits can cause OOM termination. Kubernetes does not guarantee transparent memory expansion.

questions.question: Which resource constrains aggregate resource use in a namespace?
questions.explanation: ResourceQuota limits namespace-wide consumption; LimitRange can set defaults and per-object constraints.

questions.question: Which feature matches a Pod to nodes with specified labels using simple equality constraints?
questions.explanation: nodeSelector constrains eligible nodes by labels. Service selectors choose Pods, not nodes.

questions.question: A ConfigMap is updated but a process's environment variable stays unchanged. Why?
options: Environment variables are stored in etcd only
Existing process environment is not automatically refreshed
questions.explanation: Environment values are established when the container starts; updating the source does not rewrite a running process's environment.

questions.question: Which scaling action increases the number of worker nodes?
questions.explanation: Node autoscaling changes capacity. HPA changes workload replica count and can still leave Pods Pending.

questions.question: What is the API server's main role?
options: Expose and serve the Kubernetes API
questions.explanation: The API server is the cluster API entry point; it coordinates API operations rather than serving as a registry.

questions.question: Why do controllers keep reconciling rather than running only once?
options: Real state can change after the initial deployment
questions.explanation: Ongoing reconciliation reacts to failures and configuration changes to maintain desired state.

questions.question: Which resource most directly maintains the replica count behind a typical Deployment?
questions.explanation: A Deployment manages ReplicaSets, which maintain matching Pod replicas.

questions.question: A scheduled nightly batch should finish and release resources. Which resource fits best?
questions.explanation: CronJobs create completion-oriented Jobs on a schedule, matching periodic batch processing.

questions.question: What is an appropriate StatefulSet expectation for a database?
options: Stable identities and persistent storage associations
Guaranteed zero downtime for every upgrade
questions.explanation: StatefulSets support identity and storage behavior; database resilience still requires database-specific design.

questions.question: Two independent services have different release schedules. How should they usually be packaged?
questions.explanation: Independent services benefit from separate lifecycle and scaling boundaries.

questions.question: Can two containers in the same Pod both bind the same IP and port at once?
options: Only if they share an image tag
Yes, namespaces make all ports unique
Normally no, because they share the port space
Yes, because every container always has a separate Pod IP
questions.explanation: Shared networking means port bindings can conflict inside one Pod.

questions.question: Which Linux feature controls resource consumption for container processes?
questions.explanation: Control groups account for and constrain resources. Linux namespaces provide isolation of system views.

questions.question: Which Linux feature isolates process views such as PID and network spaces?
questions.explanation: Linux namespaces isolate system views; Kubernetes namespaces are a different API organization concept.

questions.question: A Docker-built image is deployed to a containerd-based Kubernetes node. What is generally true?
options: Compatible OCI images can run without Docker Engine
Docker Engine must always be installed
The image becomes a virtual machine
questions.explanation: Image compatibility and runtime integration are separate; Docker Engine is not required for compatible images.

questions.question: Why avoid writing essential state only inside a container's writable layer?
options: It cannot be read by the process
It is not durable across container replacement
It is automatically backed up by etcd
questions.explanation: Container-local writable state is ephemeral; use appropriate persistent storage for durable data.

questions.question: A manifest sets replicas to five but status reports three ready. What does this mean?
options: Desired and observed states currently differ
questions.explanation: spec and status are different views; investigate why the requested replicas are not ready.

questions.question: A Service selector expects app=web but Pods have app=frontend. What should be corrected?
options: The mismatch between labels and selector
questions.explanation: Matching labels connect the Service to its Pods. A selector mismatch leaves no selected backends.

questions.question: What is an appropriate use of kubectl logs?
options: Read a container's standard output/error logs
questions.explanation: logs retrieves container output, not node placement or permissions.

questions.question: What is an appropriate use of kubectl exec?
options: Modify the Kubernetes scheduler source code
Run a command inside a running container
Rebuild an image in the registry automatically
questions.explanation: exec runs a command in a container subject to authorization and container capabilities.

questions.question: Does creating separate namespaces automatically isolate all network traffic?
options: Yes, all traffic is denied by default
No, network isolation needs suitable policy and enforcement
questions.explanation: Namespaces organize resources; networking behavior requires separate controls such as NetworkPolicy.

questions.question: Which setting attracts a Pod toward matching nodes using richer expressions than nodeSelector?
questions.explanation: Node affinity expresses required or preferred node placement rules.

questions.question: A matching toleration exists but the node lacks sufficient requested CPU. What happens?
options: The Pod still cannot be scheduled there on that basis
The toleration overrides all CPU checks
The CPU request becomes a memory request
questions.explanation: Tolerations address taints only; resource feasibility and other constraints still apply.

questions.question: Which object can supply default CPU requests within a namespace?
questions.explanation: LimitRange can define default requests and limits; it is not a scheduling controller.

questions.question: Why can a node with low actual CPU usage reject a Pod?
options: The scheduler uses only yesterday's logs
Existing requests can leave insufficient schedulable capacity
questions.explanation: Placement considers resource requests and allocatable capacity, not simply instantaneous usage.

questions.question: An HPA adds replicas but they remain Pending for lack of capacity. What also needs attention?
questions.explanation: More replicas need resources on nodes; workload autoscaling alone does not supply cluster capacity.

questions.question: Which Kubernetes object represents a workload's sensitive credential data?
questions.explanation: A Secret is intended for sensitive configuration, but still needs proper encryption and access controls.

questions.question: Why separate configuration from container images?
options: Reuse the same image across environments with different settings
questions.explanation: External configuration lets tested images be promoted without rebuilding for each environment.

questions.question: Which change is vertical scaling?
options: Increasing resources allocated to an application instance
questions.explanation: Vertical scaling increases per-instance resources; horizontal scaling adds instances.

questions.question: Which Service type is the usual choice for internal cluster access?
questions.explanation: ClusterIP provides an internal virtual access point; external exposure needs additional mechanisms.

questions.question: What must exist to implement an Ingress resource's routing rules?
questions.explanation: An Ingress resource is configuration; a controller implements the traffic routing.

questions.question: Which interface is associated with Kubernetes storage drivers?
questions.explanation: CSI integrates volume operations with storage providers.

questions.question: Which interface is associated with Pod networking plugins?
questions.explanation: CNI concerns container networking; storage and runtime integration use different interfaces.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a PVC?
options: Request persistent storage for a workload
Expose a Pod on the internet
questions.explanation: A claim requests storage and binds to a suitable PersistentVolume.

questions.question: Which resource commonly enables dynamic volume provisioning?
questions.explanation: StorageClasses describe storage classes and provisioners used to satisfy suitable claims.

questions.question: What happens to emptyDir data when its Pod is removed?
options: It automatically follows the replacement Pod
questions.explanation: emptyDir is scoped to the Pod lifetime, though it can survive a container restart within that Pod.

questions.question: Which question does authentication answer?
questions.explanation: Authentication establishes identity; authorization evaluates allowed actions.

questions.question: Which question does authorization answer?
options: What is the application's source code?
Is this identity allowed to perform this action?
questions.explanation: Authorization evaluates permissions after identity is established.

questions.question: What does a RoleBinding normally scope permissions to?
questions.explanation: A RoleBinding grants permissions in its own namespace, even when referencing a ClusterRole.

questions.question: Which identity is normally associated with a workload calling the Kubernetes API?
questions.explanation: ServiceAccounts supply workload identity; RBAC determines what it can do.

questions.question: A Pod shows ImagePullBackOff. Which investigation is most relevant first?
questions.explanation: ImagePullBackOff signals failed image retrieval with retries; inspect image and registry credentials/connectivity.

questions.question: A container repeatedly exits after startup. Which evidence is most useful?
questions.explanation: Logs and termination status reveal application startup errors and resource or configuration failures.

questions.question: A NetworkPolicy exists but traffic remains unrestricted. What should you verify?
options: The Secret is base64 encoded twice
The image was built by Docker
questions.explanation: Policy behavior depends on a network implementation that supports and enforces it.

questions.question: What does a Service provide when Pod IPs change?
options: A stable abstraction for reaching matching Pods
questions.explanation: Services decouple clients from transient Pod addresses.

questions.question: Which Service type exposes a port on cluster nodes?
questions.explanation: NodePort exposes a Service through a node port, subject to network reachability and policy.

questions.question: A LoadBalancer Service stays without an external IP on a local cluster. Why might that happen?
options: The Pod must be a Job
No compatible load-balancer implementation is installed
Every Service requires a public cloud account
The API server cannot store Services
questions.explanation: LoadBalancer relies on an implementation or integration to provision the external access point.

questions.question: Which feature normally resolves Kubernetes Service names?
questions.explanation: Cluster DNS, often CoreDNS, provides service discovery names.

questions.question: A Service has no ready endpoints. What should you check?
questions.explanation: Selectors choose Pods, while readiness controls normal traffic eligibility.

questions.question: What does targetPort on a Service identify?
options: The port on backend Pods receiving traffic
questions.explanation: targetPort maps Service traffic to the workload's listening port.

questions.question: What is a service mesh typically used for?
questions.explanation: A mesh adds communication controls and telemetry above basic networking.

questions.question: Does Kubernetes require a service mesh for basic Pod networking?
options: Only if there are two Pods
Yes, unless every app is stateful
questions.explanation: Basic Pod networking works through the cluster network implementation without a mesh.

questions.question: A volume cannot attach through a storage provider. Which integration is most relevant?
questions.explanation: Volume attach and mount behavior involves storage integration, commonly through CSI.

questions.question: What does ReadWriteOnce generally constrain?
options: Read-write mounting to a single node
Exactly one Pod in every situation
questions.explanation: ReadWriteOnce concerns node-level mount access; multiple Pods on that node can be possible.

questions.question: Does persistent storage automatically provide a database backup?
options: Yes, because etcd stores the database rows
No, backup and restore require separate design
Yes, every PVC is a backup
questions.explanation: Persistence survives some workload lifecycles; backups protect against deletion, corruption and other loss modes.

questions.question: What does a PV reclaim policy influence?
options: Which user owns a source repository
What happens to storage after the claim is released
Which node has the newest kernel
questions.explanation: Reclaim behavior such as Retain or Delete affects released storage; understand it before removing claims.

questions.question: A backup tool needs only to list Pods in one namespace. Which principle should guide its RBAC?
questions.explanation: Grant the specific read verbs and scope needed, rather than broad administrative access.

questions.question: A RoleBinding references a ClusterRole that allows reading Pods. Where does that binding grant the access?
questions.explanation: The referenced rule definition can be reusable while the binding remains namespaced.

questions.question: What is the role of admission control for applicable API requests?
options: Validate or mutate requests before persistence
questions.explanation: Admission follows authentication and authorization for applicable requests and can enforce policy.

questions.question: Why should a container normally avoid privileged mode?
options: It gives broader host access than most applications need
questions.explanation: Avoiding unnecessary privilege reduces the impact of compromise; use the minimum capabilities required.

questions.question: What does image signing primarily help establish?
questions.explanation: Signatures support trust in origin and integrity, but do not prove software is bug-free or vulnerability-free.

questions.question: Which control protects data in transit?
questions.explanation: TLS provides transport protection; encoding and resource sizing do not encrypt network traffic.

questions.question: A process failed and restarted. Which command option can retrieve the previous container instance's logs?
questions.explanation: --previous reads logs from the previous terminated container instance when available.

questions.question: A Pod is Pending with an unbound claim. What should you investigate?
questions.explanation: Storage claims can block scheduling; inspect events, class configuration and provisioning.

questions.question: An application returns HTTP 500 through its Service. What does that establish?
options: A request reached an HTTP endpoint, but application investigation is still needed
questions.explanation: An HTTP response indicates a working path to some endpoint; logs and application evidence are needed for root cause.

questions.question: Which evidence best separates a DNS issue from an application startup crash?
options: Name-resolution results plus Pod state and logs
questions.explanation: Different layers need different observations; DNS results and process state distinguish the symptoms.

questions.question: What should usually happen before deleting a failing Pod during investigation?
questions.explanation: Deletion can discard evidence. Inspect and preserve useful data before changing state.

questions.question: Which Kubernetes resource declares permitted network traffic for selected Pods?
questions.explanation: NetworkPolicy expresses traffic rules; RBAC governs API requests instead.

questions.question: A container only needs to serve static files. Which configuration most reduces unnecessary filesystem writes?
questions.explanation: A read-only root filesystem can reduce write capability, provided necessary writable paths are handled separately.

questions.question: What is a PersistentVolume?
options: A cluster storage resource that can satisfy a claim
questions.explanation: PVs represent storage available to workloads through claims, distinct from networking or identity objects.

questions.question: A container restarts inside the same Pod. What is generally true of its emptyDir?
options: It is always erased on any container restart
It is copied to all nodes
questions.explanation: emptyDir follows Pod lifetime rather than an individual container instance.

questions.question: A Pod can reach an IP but cannot resolve a Service name. Which area deserves attention?
questions.explanation: IP reachability with failed name resolution points toward DNS configuration or access to DNS.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of continuous integration?
options: Frequently build and test integrated code changes
questions.explanation: CI checks integration of changes through automated build and testing stages.

questions.question: How does continuous deployment differ from continuous delivery?
options: It only applies to virtual machines
Passing changes are released to production automatically
questions.explanation: Continuous delivery keeps releases ready; continuous deployment automates the production release after gates pass.

questions.question: Which practice improves consistency between tested and production artifacts?
options: Build once and promote the same immutable image
Rebuild from an unpinned branch in every environment
questions.explanation: Promoting the tested artifact avoids introducing untested differences through rebuilding.

questions.question: What is central to GitOps?
options: Only storing shell history in Git
Versioned declarative state continuously reconciled by agents
questions.explanation: GitOps combines declarative, versioned state with agent-driven reconciliation.

questions.question: Which tool is an example of a Kubernetes GitOps delivery controller?
questions.explanation: Argo CD reconciles applications from desired configuration; the other tools solve DNS, runtime and state-store concerns.

questions.question: What does a readiness probe primarily control?
options: Whether a Pod should receive Service traffic
Whether a new image is built
Whether the container must always restart
questions.explanation: Readiness failure removes normal traffic eligibility rather than itself restarting a container.

questions.question: What is a Helm chart?
options: A package of related Kubernetes templates and configuration
questions.explanation: Charts package Kubernetes application configuration; installed instances are releases.

questions.question: Which strategy initially sends a limited portion of traffic to a new version?
questions.explanation: Canary releases limit initial exposure and use evidence before broadening rollout.

questions.question: A team requires human approval before production release but automated preparation. Which approach fits?
questions.explanation: Continuous delivery can automate readiness for release while retaining a human production decision.

questions.question: Why is a successful image build insufficient evidence of a successful release?
options: Runtime behavior and user-facing health can still fail
questions.explanation: Configuration, dependencies and production conditions can fail even when build steps succeeded.

questions.question: A manual cluster change is repeatedly undone by a controller tracking Git. Why?
questions.explanation: GitOps controllers can reconcile live drift back to the configured desired state.

questions.question: Does reverting a Git commit automatically reverse a database migration?
options: Only if the cluster has CoreDNS
No, data changes need their own recovery plan
questions.explanation: Configuration rollback and data rollback are different operations; migrations require deliberate recovery design.

questions.question: What is a blue-green release?
options: Change Pod colors in a dashboard
Run all versions in one container process
Delete the cluster and rebuild it
Switch traffic between old and new deployment environments
questions.explanation: Blue-green keeps separate environments and changes the traffic target after validation.

questions.question: What does maxSurge allow during a Deployment rolling update?
options: Temporary extra Pods above desired replicas
questions.explanation: maxSurge controls temporary additional capacity used during a rollout.

questions.question: What does a liveness probe failure eventually trigger after its threshold?
options: Container restart according to probe behavior
questions.explanation: Liveness checks detect conditions where restarting may help; thresholds govern failure action.

questions.question: Which probe is useful for protecting a slowly starting application?
questions.explanation: A startup probe delays normal liveness and readiness probing until startup succeeds.

questions.question: Which pipeline stage should create the distributable container artifact?
questions.explanation: The build stage produces an image that can be tested, scanned, stored and promoted.

questions.question: Where should desired configuration normally be changed in a GitOps workflow?
options: Only by editing a running container
Only by rewriting etcd files directly
In a public DNS TXT record
In the version-controlled source through the team's review process
questions.explanation: Updating the declared source makes the change reviewable and prevents reconciliation undoing it as drift.

questions.question: What does drift mean in a GitOps context?
options: Live state differs from declared desired state
A PV has more free space
The cluster is in another region
questions.explanation: Drift is a mismatch between intended and running configuration, often caused by out-of-band changes.

questions.question: What is a Helm release?
options: An installed instance of a chart
questions.explanation: A chart is the package; a release is a particular installation with values and history.

questions.question: Which tool applies overlays to base Kubernetes manifests?
questions.explanation: Kustomize composes and customizes resource configuration using bases and overlays.

questions.question: A readiness probe fails. What is the expected immediate purpose of this signal?
options: Stop normal Service traffic to the unready Pod
questions.explanation: Readiness governs availability for traffic; it does not itself mandate a restart.

questions.question: Why is checking a fragile external dependency in liveness potentially harmful?
options: A dependency outage can cause unnecessary restart loops
It changes every Service to LoadBalancer
questions.explanation: Liveness should reflect whether restarting the container is useful, not merely whether a dependency is temporarily unavailable.

questions.question: A Deployment rollback restores the old image but errors remain. Why is that possible?
options: Persistent data or external dependencies may still be incompatible
Rollbacks always erase all database changes
questions.explanation: Workload revision rollback does not reverse all external state, data migrations or dependency changes.

questions.question: Which signal is most suited to tracking an error rate over time?
questions.explanation: Metrics represent numerical observations over time, making rates and trends measurable.

questions.question: Which signal connects operations across a request's path through several services?
questions.explanation: Traces link spans across a request, showing relationships and latency contributions.

questions.question: What is Prometheus primarily used for?
questions.explanation: Prometheus is a monitoring and metrics system, not a scheduler or build service.

questions.question: Does cloud native require hosting in a public cloud?
options: Yes, unless all apps use Windows
No, the principles also apply on premises
questions.explanation: Cloud native describes architecture and operational approaches, not a mandatory hosting location.

questions.question: What is an important microservices trade-off?
options: Every service must share one database schema
questions.explanation: Separate services can evolve independently but create network, consistency and operational challenges.

questions.question: Which is a valid open-source contribution?
options: Improving documentation with the project's contribution process
questions.explanation: Documentation, testing and constructive issues are valuable contributions alongside code.

questions.question: What is OpenTelemetry primarily intended to provide?
options: Vendor-neutral instrumentation and telemetry collection/export components
A complete mandatory dashboard and storage backend
questions.explanation: OpenTelemetry helps produce and route telemetry; backends supply storage, analysis and visualization.

questions.question: What is the relationship between an SLI and an SLO?
options: They always refer to CPU hardware
An SLI measures behavior; an SLO sets a target
An SLO is a container runtime and an SLI a volume
questions.explanation: SLIs quantify service behavior, while SLOs define intended performance or reliability levels.

questions.question: What does an error budget express?
options: Tolerated unreliability within a target period
questions.explanation: An error budget derives from a reliability objective and its allowed failure proportion.

questions.question: Which statement about serverless is accurate?
options: Infrastructure still exists but more of its operation is abstracted
questions.explanation: Serverless shifts operational responsibilities; it does not eliminate physical or virtual compute.

questions.question: Which pattern can improve resilience during dependency failures?
options: Bounded retries with timeouts and appropriate backoff
questions.explanation: Bound retries and timeouts prevent uncontrolled waiting and retry amplification.

questions.question: What do CNCF maturity levels primarily describe?
questions.explanation: Maturity stages describe project development and governance criteria, not universal fitness.

questions.question: A dashboard needs visualizations of data from multiple backends. Which tool fits?
questions.explanation: Grafana visualizes queried data; collection and storage can be supplied by other systems.

questions.question: What is a log best described as?
options: A count of desired replicas only
A record of an event or message
questions.explanation: Logs capture event details and complement numerical metrics and request traces.

questions.question: Which example is horizontal scaling?
questions.explanation: Horizontal scaling adds instances; vertical scaling changes resources per instance.

questions.question: Why is simply containerizing a monolith insufficient to guarantee resilience?
options: Failure handling and operational design are still required
questions.explanation: Packaging is only one part of the system; resilience needs appropriate architecture and operations.

questions.question: What should a useful open-source bug report include?
options: Reproduction steps, environment and sanitized evidence
questions.explanation: Maintainers need reproducible, relevant information without exposed secrets to diagnose issues.

questions.question: What is a Kubernetes SIG?
options: A special interest group focused on a subject area
questions.explanation: SIGs organize Kubernetes community collaboration around particular areas of responsibility.
